Maryland’s highest court heard arguments on an appeal Monday that will affect 1,300 lawsuits filed under the Child Victims Act.
The 2023 law effectively eliminated time barriers for someone to file a court claim of institutional sex abuse. At issue are the roughly 1,300 cases in which the alleged sexual assaults took place before 1982, a time when the state had absolute immunity from lawsuits. The Supreme Court of Maryland is being asked to decide if the General Assembly, when it passed the landmark 2023 law, clearly and knowingly waived that immunity.
The article is republished from Maryland Matters.
Jonathan Massey, attorney for a plaintiff known only as J.C., said the waiver of damage caps in the 2023 law are proof of the legislature’s intent.
The change “is the waiver of state sovereign immunity, and make changes that assume there will be a damages cap, assuming there will be liability to the state, right? That’s why you need a damages cap because there’s going to be liability to the state. I don’t think the legislature was silent in 2023 on the issue of sovereign immunity,” Massey said during oral arguments.
Monday’s appeal involves a claim of sexual abuse from 1977, when J.C. was a patient at the old Prince George’s Hospital Center, where she claimed a doctor molested her during a stay there.
Lawyers for the state argued that the state at the time was protected by sovereign immunity. Prior to 1982, the state could not face civil lawsuits, and the state’s lawyers asked a Prince George’s County judge to dismiss the case on those grounds.
Attorneys representing the state filed roughly 200 motions to dismiss cases involving claims before July 1, 1982. The state has argued that the legislature must expressly waive the 40-year old immunity provision, something they said the 2023 law did not do.
Judges at the Circuit Court level granted four motions at the time the appeal was filed with the state’s highest court.
The Prince George’s County court denied the state’s motion without a hearing or explanation. But judges in Frederick County and Baltimore City have agreed with the state. Each dismissed cases under the sovereign immunity argument.
The Supreme Court’s ruling on the issue comes with a dollar sign attached.
Cases involving allegations occurring before 1982 comprise about 11% of the 12,000 cases that have been filed under the Child Victims Act. The 2023 law capped damages against the state at $890,000 per occurrence, but the definition of an “occurrence” is still being debated.
The full extent of the state’s potential liability has never been publicly stated. A rough estimate shows potentially budget-busting consequences.
If each plaintiff alleged just one occurrence and received the maximum award, the potential liability to the state could be about $11 billion. That estimate is nearly four times the structural budget gap projected for the fiscal 2028 budget to be introduced in January.
The potential payout could go up if a court or jury defines “occurrence” as each instance of abuse, rather than bundling instances based on any number of related circumstances. Settlements could reduce the potential liability.
If lawyers for the state are successful in getting the pre-1982 cases blocked, it would reduce the state’s potential liability by “more than a billion dollars,” the Office of the Attorney General argued in a filing earlier this year.

I don’t know about you, but I have days, weeks, and months when my running is challenging.
Sometimes that challenge arises when you’re coming back from an injury or an offseason, while other times it can be due to particularly busy or stressful times in life. When that time comes, even getting out the door feels daunting. When that’s the case, a little nudge can go a long way to getting back on track.
I find that this one small promise can help me quickly return to real running: 7×7.
No fewer than four times so far this decade, I’ve gone to my tried-and-true crutch: I run seven miles a day for seven straight days. It’s a small idea, but it’s worked every time.
Every one of those times, I was in a place where even the first seven-mile run felt daunting, but I told myself I was going to do it. I got out the door, and then again the next day, and the day after that, until I’d completed seven days. If I had to walk the second half of the week, that’s fine. If I was slow as all get out, it didn’t matter. The point was to get out there and cover the ground.
After I completed that commitment, I’d gotten over that hump, that activation energy, that dark hill that stood in front of me, I found myself on a ridge I could run along. I’d renewed a habit. I could run for an hour. That was fine. If I could run for an hour every day for a week — no matter how I felt, how tired I was, or what the weather was — then I could run for an hour on any day that followed.
And while 7×7 itself was a small commitment, it actually stood in lieu of a larger one hiding behind it, and that was a recommitment to myself as a runner. It helped me re-identify as a runner and prioritize that time in my daily life.
Now, 7×7 might not be a magical commitment for you, but I bet you can find ways to jump-start your own running if you need to. Here are some thoughts on how you might do that successfully.
- Keep it short. If you’re having a rough patch in your running, it might be too much to commit to running every day for a year. But it could be five days, two weeks, every day during a vacation, or whatever timeframe works for you.
- Keep the bar low (enough). If you’re trying to overcome a hill, don’t make your challenge a mountain. While seven miles of running might seem daunting to me on the first day of 7×7, I know from decades of running that an hour is totally doable, even if it’s double what I might run during a slump. For me, even upping that to 10 miles a day might go from restarting a good habit to physically challenging.
- Make it concrete. Have numbers. If it’s going to be running a certain number of days, or if it’s a certain number of miles in a week, whatever it is, establish a concrete goal because you hit it or you don’t.
- Bonus: Keep it a little lighthearted. I wish I had a game or an explicitly fun aspect to 7×7, but the name by itself will have to be lighthearted enough. Surely you can create something more lighthearted than I have.

Bloom spoke to the media during the General Managers Meetings at the Aria Resort and Casino in Las Vegas on Tuesday to recount the 2026 season and look ahead. Just as with every other team and its baseball executives, there’s a bit more urgency than usual at this time of the year, with the Collective Bargaining Agreement set to expire on Dec. 1, meaning there will likely be more free-agent and trade activity during this month than most years.
Bloom, however, is seemingly more concerned with the overall picture for the Cardinals and trying to address areas across the entire organization.
“Certainly for us, we’re working on our staff. We're working to talk to agents about their players and free agency,” Bloom said. “We're working to talk to other teams. So there's really three fronts we're operating on.”
Asked by reporters if there was any urgency about fixing the roster and coaching staff before Dec. 1, Bloom didn’t necessarily seem rushed by the upcoming deadline.
“A lot of these things are just things that you want to be out in front of as much as you can,” Bloom said. “So at least for us, it hasn't really changed much.”
Bloom’s Cardinals showed a lot of promise in his first full season at the helm, given that the club traded major players from the previous rosters last offseason, including Willson Contreras, Sonny Gray and Nolan Arenado. The breakouts from JJ Wetherholt, who finished third in NL Rookie of the Year voting in 2026, and Jordan Walker and the continued development from the likes of Alec Burleson, Andre Pallante and Michael McGreevy have only added optimism for 2027 and beyond.
Now comes the task of supplementing a roster that flirted with an NL Wild Card spot, whether via free agency and trades or a rapidly improving farm system.
“I think we need to do a lot more things that are consistent with what we started doing last year to keep going, to keep integrating other players, keep pushing to get the most out of things, keep looking to acquire more pieces for the core and then to put the right pieces around,” Bloom said.
That next wave of young Cardinals talent could take on an even more pronounced role in 2027. Beyond the aforementioned players, youngsters like Joshua Báez and Leo Bernal, who already showed promise in the Majors, while top prospects Rainiel Rodriguez (MLB Pipeline’s No. 1 Cardinals prospect) and Liam Doyle (No. 2 prospect) figure to be impact talents soon.
“There's a couple different angles that we can look at. One is making sure -- whether they’re players that have already debuted with us or players that hopefully that debut is in the relatively near future -- making sure we have lanes for them,” Bloom said. “We don't want to hand them anything, but we want to make sure we have lanes for them to break in, and if they have broken in, to be able to thrive.”
That other lane is looking via free agency and trade to supplement this growing list of young Cardinals that could form the next great St. Louis team.
“There's also looking outside the organization from a trade standpoint as to whether there are players who might be able to join that core for the long haul, whether in a front-and-center role or a supporting role,” Bloom said. “That's really important, too. States are counting on battery farms. Some towns don’t want them.
A battery storage facility sits in front of wind turbines near Palm Springs, California. States and utilities are building battery farms but many communities oppose them. (Photo by Mario Tama/Getty Images)
SNOQUALMIE, Wash. — In the race to meet the nation’s growing power demands, states and utilities are rapidly building new “battery farms” that can store energy for when customers need it most. But as the facilities grow, so too does community opposition.
The systems store banks of batteries in buildings or shipping containers. While they can take many forms, developers are increasingly building large, multi-acre projects designed to meet the needs of local utilities.
The electricity stored by such systems nationwide has grown tenfold since 2022, and it’s projected to double again by the end of 2028. State lawmakers and renewable energy advocates say battery storage is urgently needed to stabilize the grid and support the transition to clean power.
But in some communities, residents are wary of proposals to build industrial battery systems in their neighborhoods, noting that battery fires can produce toxic smoke and are difficult to extinguish. As the backlash has grown, nearly 200 communities have passed or proposed moratoriums to block battery farms from being built near them.
Backers say modern systems are designed to be much safer than previous versions, with data showing that fire risk has dropped significantly. But some industry leaders fear the perception of danger — along with a rising tide of community activism stirred by the buildout of data centers — could threaten an industry that’s becoming integral to the nation’s energy future.
‘Meteoric growth’
Most energy storage on the U.S. grid takes the form of battery energy storage systems, commonly known as BESS. Such facilities host banks of batteries, typically lithium-ion — a technology that has become more capable and cost-effective with the development of electric vehicles.
At present, battery storage capacity nationwide exceeds 50 gigawatts, up from just 5 gigawatts at the beginning of 2022. Another 54 gigawatts is slated to come online in the next two and a half years. That projected total of more than 100 gigawatts would be enough to power roughly 75 million homes, although battery farms are designed to provide electricity for one to four hours, as opposed to the more continuous supply of conventional power plants.
“The meteoric growth is continuing,” said Noah Roberts, executive director of the U.S. Energy Storage Coalition, an industry group. “For state policymakers who are focused on the energy transition and decarbonizing the grid, (battery) storage is essential.”
Policymakers and energy planners have increasingly pushed for battery farms as more renewable energy sources have come online. Solar farms, for instance, can produce massive amounts of cheap electricity during the afternoon hours — but peak demand is in the evening, when people get home from work and turn on household appliances.
With batteries on the grid, that surplus solar energy can be stored and saved for when it’s needed, instead of firing up more costly “peaker” gas plants to meet evening demand.

Much of the midterm “blue tsunami” came from diverse, enthusiastic young voters with financial struggles who flocked to the polls, and also Trump voters sitting out the election, according to two experts analyzing turnout in a handful of states with detailed results.
The results, they say, could mean a mandate for bringing costs down and more power for young Latinos, but also a danger for Democrats if Republicans rally back to the polls in 2028.
“It looks like more Trump voters who didn’t vote Republican stayed home rather than switching (to Democrats),” said Lenny Bronner, founder of Broome Street Labs and a data scientist formerly with the Washington Post, based on his analysis of 13 states with detailed results.
“Those voters are easier for the GOP to win back than those who chose a Democratic candidate,” Bronner said.
Bronner estimated 75% of Democratic gains came from a turnout gap and about 20% from Republicans switching sides and voting for Democrats.
His analysis included turnout data for Texas, Georgia, South Carolina, Colorado, New Mexico, Virginia, North Carolina, Arkansas, Iowa, Florida, West Virginia, Minnesota and Michigan. The share of Democrats’ gain that came from a turnout gap ranged from 40% for Texas to 133% for Michigan among the states he studied; some states had only partial detailed results.
Bronner wrote on X (formerly Twitter) that partial results in Texas showed that voters flipped their ballots more than expected; 45% of Democratic gains there came from voters switching away from Republicans. “So far, Texas is the only state where our model indicates that persuasion explains more of Democrats net gain than turnout does!” he wrote.
A University of Florida political science professor, Michael McDonald, also saw a turnout surge for young voters faced with high grocery bills, student loan debt and sluggish wages, based on detailed results from Georgia and Colorado. Trump’s older voter constituency was more likely to stay home, he wrote in a Substack post.

The swirl of sex-and-spying allegations around Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is raising a worrying question: Could trouble at the chipmaker spread through the tightly connected financial network Nvidia has built to support the artificial intelligence boom?
Serious problems with Nvidia could do far-reaching economic and financial damage. The company has made hundreds of billions of dollars in financial commitments to other firms to help the industry grow, earning it the nickname the "central bank of AI." The Federal Reserve and other financial institutions are closely watching the AI buildout to monitor for the possibility that an unexpected event could destabilize the global financial system.
Even back in July Fed officials were discussing the possibility of of a "broad-based repricing of assets" in the event of problems in the AI sector.
A rerun of the 2007-2008 financial crisis isn't likely, according to analysts and current and former financial officials. Nvidia isn't "too big to fail in a bank sense at all," said Sheila Bair, a former government regulator who ran the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. Unlike a troubled bank, Nvidia isn't vulnerable to a sudden loss of confidence and would still produce a product customers want to buy even if something went wrong. And its massive equity gives it a cushion.
But regulators need to watch carefully for exposure by the banks and the wider financial system to Nvidia and other firms like it, Bair said.
"Nvidia going down would be a pretty seismic event," she said.
Investors still have high hopes for Nvidia, which reports earnings on Tuesday. Analysts expect its revenue to more than double in the current fiscal year, and then to roughly double again over the following two years, according to LSEG data. But with Huang under scrutiny by the FBI, Congress, and Nvidia's board over his relationship with a woman who The New York Times reported was suspected of spying for China, analysts see a wide range of outcomes as suddenly possible, including the potential removal of Huang, who co-founded the company in 1993.
The company didn't immediately respond to a request for comment. Nvidia's board has expressed confidence in its CEO.

Its stock recovered Wednesday, rising more than 4% as of midday. Still, people who closely track the financial flows underlying AI say that even sharper losses by Nvidia likely wouldn't trigger the kind of systemic problems that regulators guard against.

What you do to recover between runs matters just as much as the miles themselves. But knowing what your body needs isn’t always straightforward. Should you head out for an easy run or take the day off? Is that soreness normal, or a sign of an injury about to derail everything? And which recovery tools are actually worth the hype?
This guide helps you navigate those decisions, starting with the fundamentals. Plus, we’ll help you choose a training plan to ease back into running after a race, your offseason, or an injury (both minor and burdensome).
Whether you’re bouncing back from a tough workout or gearing up for your next training block, start planning your recovery here.
Recovery Fundamentals
Recovery doesn’t have to be complicated, but it does require giving the basics as much attention as your workouts. Easy runs, rest days, postrun fueling, and sleep all help your body manage the work you’re putting in. That means keeping most of your miles at a pace where you can comfortably hold a conversation, rather than turning every run into another hard effort.

It also means taking at least one full day off from training each week—and more if you’re new to running or need extra recovery.
What you do after a run matters, too: Carbohydrates replenish energy stores, protein supports muscle repair, and sufficient sleep gives your body time to recover and rebuild.
Need some postrun fueling inspiration? Try one of these:
- Toasted bagel with cream cheese, smoked salmon, and sliced pickled beets
- A bowl of cereal with milk
- Two hard-boiled eggs with a glass of tomato juice

Managing Soreness and Fatigue
Sore legs after a tough workout can come with the territory. But knowing when to take it easy—and when to stop running—isn’t always obvious. Before you push through discomfort, pay attention to how it feels, whether it’s improving, and how it affects the way you move.
Delayed-onset muscle soreness, or DOMS, typically develops within 24 to 72 hours after a challenging workout and gradually fades with time and movement. Here’s how to recognize normal soreness and spot signs that may indicate something more serious.
Typical muscle soreness tends to:
- Feel like a dull ache or stiffness
- Improve with stretching and recovery tools
- Dissipate after a few days
If your soreness isn’t affecting your day-to-day and you can move normally, a short, easy run may help ease the discomfort.
Signs of a possible injury include:
- Sharp or stabbing pain
- Pain that lasts longer than three days (even if it’s just when you’re running)
- Swelling or bruising
- Numbness, tingling, weakness, or feeling like a joint might give out
- Pain that interferes with your running gait and then eventually your walking gait
If you notice these warning signs, stop running and seek guidance from a healthcare professional rather than trying to push through.

To be at the frontier of quantum computing, industry-relevant applications demand both computational quality and speed. Speed matters because a quantum computer delivers its answer in samples: each run of a quantum circuit returns one result. Scale and quality enable increasingly complex computations, but speed determines whether these demanding workloads can be completed in practical timeframes and at a reasonable cost.

When winter arrives, it’s tempting to put your running goals on hold until the temperatures warm up, the days get longer, and the roads clear. Cold temperatures make it harder to leave a warm bed, while snow and ice can turn a familiar route into a much slower—and more slippery—run.
For months at a time, Michelle Baxter’s running routes in Anchorage, Alaska, were covered in packed snow and ice. After a snowstorm, plows could take days to reach every neighborhood, and by then, cars had compressed the fallen snow onto the roads. Even after the plows came through, the slick surface often remained.
Baxter—now an RRCA- and V.02-certified run coach—spent 15 years living in Alaska and training through winters like these, figuring out how to keep running through harsh, unmotivating conditions.
She trained for 12 marathons in that time, continuing to build fitness year after year. Eventually, she even achieved her most ambitious running goal: breaking three hours in the marathon. After eight years of attempting to break the barrier—and a heartbreakingly close 3:01:14 at Humpy’s Marathon in Anchorage in August 2021—Baxter finally ran a 2:58:24 at the California International Marathon in December 2021. She has since lowered her PR to 2:56:57 at the Indianapolis Monumental Marathon.
Your winter running routes may not be covered in snow and ice for six months straight, but chances are you’ll face your own challenges as the temperature drops in the coming weeks and months. The good news: Baxter’s experience can help you navigate tough terrain and make the most of your training.
Here’s how you can put her lessons to work this winter so when the ice thaws, you’re ready to run your fastest race yet.
Find Gear That Makes Winter Running Manageable
What you wear can make or break a winter run, Baxter says. When you’re too cold, too warm, or worried about taking a spill around every tight corner, it’s hard to focus on any other aspect of the run. Baxter spent years figuring out what works, and her gear advice starts with two essentials: finding reliable footwear and appropriate layers for the conditions.
→Getting a Grip on Slippery Surfaces
In Anchorage, finding reliable footing was Baxter’s biggest winter challenge. She initially resisted buying studded shoes, assuming they wouldn’t make much difference. But once she tried them, she was surprised by how much more confident she felt in every step.
For packed snow, Baxter often wore regular trainers fitted with screws in the outsoles, which she added herself.
On sheer ice, Baxter preferred shoes made with built-in carbide studs; she swears by the Icebug brand. “You can wear these shoes and make a 90-degree turn and feel so confident running on ice—like sheer ice,” Baxter says. “They were a game-changer for me.”
You may not encounter sheets of ice on your regular running routes, but consider the conditions you encounter most often and look for an option suited to them.
Now living in Minnesota, Baxter says she reaches for studded shoes if she expects at least half of a run to cover potentially snowy or icy ground. She notes that while the shoes may be slightly less comfortable than your normal trainers, protecting your body from harm is the number-one priority during the winter months of training.
“I just think it’s worth it to feel confident running on the slippery surfaces and not risk injuring yourself,” she says.

How a 28-Day Window Becomes $81 Billion
To get run-rate revenue, Anthropic takes consumption fees from the trailing 28 days and multiplies them by 13. It then adds monthly subscription fees multiplied by 12. Because of that growth, one strong month can quickly push the reported figure up.
So the October jump is impressive, but it may not last. The filing says the figure does not replace GAAP revenue, is not a forecast, has not been independently verified, and can swing with holiday usage. It can also include amounts from customers later found violating usage policies.

A New York City sightseeing helicopter on a maintenance flight made an emergency landing on Tuesday at a New Jersey cargo port after the pilot reported possible engine trouble.
Two people were aboard the Bell 206L-4 helicopter when it came down on a road at the Port Jersey Marine Terminal in Bayonne, across the Hudson River from Manhattan, around 8:55 a.m., the Federal Aviation Administration said.
No injuries were reported, the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey said. Messages seeking comment were left for the helicopter’s operator, FlyNYON.
Video of the scene shows part of the helicopter’s tail sitting on the road about 30 feet (9 meters) from the aircraft, which was manufactured in 1999, according to FAA records.

Insured losses from the wildfires that plagued Washington for nearly half the summer are nearing $1 billion from roughly 3,500 claims, far exceeding projections of $600 million in September for what has become the most expensive wildfires in state history.
Those figures encompass all wildfires in the state from June to present, but most losses are from the Spokane Complex Fire, comprised of the Old Trails, Fairview and Autumn Lane fires that destroyed roughly 900 structures. An analysis from property data provider Cotality identified 5,256 properties that sustained at least some damage, of which 96% were single-family residences.
The fires, which ignited on Aug. 1, grew to 10,000-acres-plus, burned 19 days and prompted evacuations of more than 65,000 people.
The biggest insured loss came from the Old Trails Fire, which occurred in the wildland-urban interface, with an estimated $665 million in insured losses.
The blaze was studied by the Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety researchers, who looked into how factors such as structure spacing, connective fuels and building components interact under the fire weather conditions.
The IBHS research on the Old Trails Fire in Spokane County, which destroyed 615 structures, shows connective fuels like combustible fences and mulch created pathways for fire to reach homes.
Researchers documented damage and fire-spread pathways at 132 structures across nine areas, identifying vulnerabilities involving windows, decks, building materials and other structural features.
Aerial imagery captured just six hours after ignition showed multiple fire outbreaks burning simultaneously. That stretched firefighting resources and left crews unable to protect all the threatened structures, according to the report.

Companies with such long records will be reluctant to break their streaks. A fine company to consider is consumer products giant Procter & Gamble (PG -0.59%), which recently yielded 2.6%.
In October, Procter & Gamble declared its latest dividend, noting that "P&G has been paying a dividend for 136 consecutive years since its incorporation in 1890 and has increased its dividend for 70 consecutive years. This reinforces our commitment to return cash to shareowners, many of whom rely on the steady, reliable income earned with their investment in P&G."
Here's a look at why you might want to invest in P&G -- or why you might not want to.
PG Procter & Gamble
NYSE · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/11/26
Why buy Procter & Gamble stock?
Here are reasons to be a P&G fan:
- It has a super-strong portfolio of valuable brands, such as Always, Ambi Pur, Ariel, Bounty, Charmin, Crest, Dawn, Downy, Fairy, Febreze, Gain, Gillette, Head & Shoulders, Lenor, Olay, Oral-B, Pampers, Pantene, SK-II, Tide, Vicks, and Whisper.
- Its dividend is still growing at a respectable clip, averaging annual gains of 4.6% over the past five years and nearly 5% over the past decade.
- That 70-year streak of dividend increases is rather remarkable, considering it goes back to the 1950s and spans multiple crashes and recessions, when many companies shrank or suspended their payouts.
- It has recently been gaining market share in China, which bodes well for its top and bottom lines.
Why pass on Procter & Gamble?
Of course, investing in P&G is not a no-brainer decision. Consider that:
- Ongoing inflation can provide a headwind, as can unfavorable currency translations. (P&G is a very global company, generating about half of its revenue abroad, largely in Europe.)
- Shares are not exactly bargain-priced at recent levels, though they are rather reasonably priced, with a recent forward-looking price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 24. That's a mite above the five-year average of 23.
- The stock is not likely to grow very fast. Its average annual gain over the past decade is 9% -- though it's up 20% year to date.
I alluded earlier to a key reason why you might want to invest in Procter & Gamble sooner rather than later: It's a steady performer when the economy sinks. (After all, people will still buy shampoos and diapers, whether the economy is booming or busting.) If you're worried about a looming stock market crash, this would be a solid portfolio holding with which to weather one.

Documents stored within Navatar CRM.

Other connected document management systems.
Shared drives.

Wells Fargo Q3 Earnings Beat on Higher NII & Lower Expenses
Wells Fargo reported third-quarter 2026 earnings per share of $1.87, which surpassed the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $1.85. In the prior-year quarter, the company reported EPS of $1.73.
Results benefited from higher net interest income (NII) and lower noninterest expenses. Growth in loan and deposit balances was another positive. However, higher provisions and lower noninterest income were headwinds.
The company's net income (GAAP basis) was $5.95 billion, representing a 6.5% increase from the prior-year quarter.
Revenues Improve, Expenses Decline
Total revenues were $21.87 billion, which missed the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $22.15 billion. Nevertheless, the top line increased 2.0% from the year-ago quarter.
NII was $12.52 billion, up 4.7% year over year. The increase was driven by higher loan and investment securities balances, fixed-rate asset repricing and growth in the Markets business. These were partially offset by higher deposit costs and the impact of lower interest rates on floating-rate assets.
The net interest margin (on a taxable-equivalent basis) contracted 18 basis points (bps) year over year to 2.43%.
Non-interest income declined 1.4% year over year to $9.35 billion. The decline was due to lower trading gains, reduced mortgage banking income and weaker equity investment gains, along with lower lease income following the sale of the company's rail car leasing business in the first quarter of 2026. Has Trade Desk Stock Become A Different Bet?
For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.
Trade Desk (TTD) stock trades at 22.8 times earnings. That puts its valuation about level with the S&P 500 at 21.9, even though the company posted flat sales in fiscal Q3 2026. Shareholders paying that multiple are likely betting that growth comes back. They need to understand what they are buying, because the company’s priorities have changed. On its fiscal Q3 2025 call, management described CTV, its connected-TV advertising, as its largest and fastest-growing channel. The company now emphasizes something else. So what is it?
Trade Desk Now Talks Up Its AI Agents
Management now pitches AI agents that set up and fine-tune ad campaigns, citing internal figures that show better results for advertisers. During the fiscal Q3 2026 call on November 9, 2026, management said it believes “agentic workflows can materially change the productivity of advertising teams.” Trade Desk tested its upgraded AI model, Koa, across 62 campaigns. The model improved CPA, the cost an advertiser pays for each result, by a median of 21%.
AI itself is not new for management: in February 2026 it said it would discuss an agentic AI framework for partners, and in August 2026 it said it had added “tons of AI capabilities.” What has changed is CTV. In August 2026, on the fiscal Q2 2026 call, management cited over 50% CTV growth in both EMEA and APAC. The company still discusses CTV. Management listed it alongside agentic AI and measurement among its highest return opportunities on the latest call, but executives no longer highlight CTV’s growth.
Video Is Still The Biggest Channel
Video, which includes CTV, is still Trade Desk’s biggest channel, at a low 50s percent share of the business in fiscal Q3 2026, management said. But video is not the fastest-growing channel: audio, around 7% of the business, posted much stronger growth than any other channel. A year ago, management’s claim was about CTV alone, not all of video.
Growth has faded across the entire company. Trade Desk reported revenue of $736 million in fiscal Q3 2026, down 0.5% from a year earlier. That decline followed a 17.7% rise in fiscal Q3 2025, and growth slowed in every intervening quarter. With video representing about half of the business, Trade Desk’s sales are hard to grow quickly unless video also grows.
Management also measures the AI tools by how clients use them. It said Koa optimizations are now switched on for 22% more strategies than before, and that more than 100 advertisers have tested Audience Unlimited, a tool that uses AI to find the audiences most likely to respond.
Should You Worry About Trade Desk’s Results?
So far, the numbers give a holder more to worry about than to cheer, because the flat quarter had help from one-off and election-year business. Management said the fiscal Q3 2026 results beat its own outlook. That included a benefit to revenue of about 3 percentage points from business with a strategic partner that it does not expect to recur, and management said the business did better than it expected even without it.
Political advertising around the U.S. midterm elections provided additional support, representing a mid-single-digit share of the business. Management said that revenue in election years has historically fallen about 25% from the fourth quarter to the first, and told investors to keep that in mind for the first quarter of 2027.

XLE tracks the Energy Select Sector Index, which represents the energy companies inside the S&P 500. If you loved the Topo Ultraventure 4 (review), the Ultraventure 5 will feel familiar. Worsening flooding from king tides and rising sea level has prompted one Fort Lauderdale city commissioner to draft a plan to raise roads, elevate seawalls and offer financial support for flood barriers on homes.
Commissioner Steve Glassman said his phone was blowing up in the last two weeks as king tide flooding hit streets that had never flooded before, closing access to homes and business, the South Florida Sun Sentinel and other news sites reported.
Glassman has asked city staff to come up with a framework within 90 days that could help alleviate the growing problem. Fort Lauderdale already is investing in extensive stormwater drainage and flood-mitigation programs, but the commissioner said those long-term projects need to be augmented with work that can have an immediate impact, the newspaper reported.
City staff are examining Glassman’s proposal and other ways to mitigate flooding, a spokesperson told the Sentinel.
The king tides are a regular occurrence in south Florida but they have worsened in recent weeks thanks to heavy rainfall, rising seas and offshore winds that pushed seawater into low-lying areas, weather and news reports have indicated. Flooding in early November was so severe that it forced the closure of a rehabilitation hospital in Melbourne, Florida.

The New World screwworm has made a comeback in the US after months of relatively muted cases, thanks in large part to milder temperatures and humidity that are encouraging the deadly livestock parasite’s activity.
More than 40 cases of screwworm have been confirmed so far in November, already making it the worst month since the pest first appeared in Texas earlier this year, according to the US Department of Agriculture. Cases began accelerating in October, when the pest spread to Arizona for the first time.
There have been a total of nearly 130 cases in the US, with more than 60 currently active.
When screwworm first arrived in the US in June, “a lot of us were like, ‘Okay, yep, we’re in for a rough summer,'” said Caleb Hubbard, an assistant professor of urban entomology at New Mexico State University. But there were much fewer cases than feared.
In hindsight, the US had just gotten lucky: Screwworm flies like warm weather, but not the extreme above-100F days that Texas and New Mexico faced in July and August. The parasite is less active in such temperatures, both in movement and in reproduction. Colder temperatures — below 59F — also make the flies more sluggish.
“It was something that I think we all were like, ‘Whew, we got through it, we’re all good,'” Hubbard said of the hotter summer days. “But as temperatures have started to decline, at least in the Southwest, we’re kind of in this Goldilocks zone right now” for the screwworm.
The parasite’s life cycle can be as short as two to three weeks in ideal conditions, above 80F — but below 100F — with high humidity, according to Texas A&M University. Screwworms only mate once, but during that short window in that temperature zone they are more active, with greater opportunities for the population to grow.
Extreme heat in Texas when the fly first arrived created “actually a pretty hostile environment,” said Phillip Kaufman, an entomology professor at Texas A&M. “We finally have started getting some cooler weather — not cold, but cooler weather here, and there has been an uptick in rain events, particularly over Arizona, New Mexico, and West Texas,” exactly where the fly has been detected.
The spread to Arizona is “part of a natural progression” as the pest pushes westward from Texas, and northward from Mexico, Mykaela Martin, public information officer for the Arizona Department of Agriculture, said in an email.
Despite the rapid acceleration, the outbreak is still minuscule compared to the 95,000 cases that the US reckoned with in its worst outbreak in 1972. Cases at that time stretched across all of Texas, up into Oklahoma and as far west as California.
The USDA to a large degree was able to contain the current outbreak through the summer with livestock movement controls, a monitoring and surveillance program, and the dispersing of sterile flies for curbing the screwworm’s reproduction.
The agency said in an emailed statement that the current weather patterns are “certainly conditions that could cause an increase in fly survivability, though it is difficult to determine a sole reason” for the recent jump in cases.
Other explanations for the uptick in infections and wild flies caught in the USDA’s traps include the movement of animals. The fly does not travel very far on its own and depends on either livestock or wildlife to spread.

I’ve spent the last several years testing running watches, from the $800 flagships with topographical maps and training-readiness scores to the ones that do almost nothing except tell you how fast you’re going. Both have their place.
“Basic” has become an insult, and I’d like us to cut that right the heck out. A basic running watch isn’t a cheap, crappy watch—it’s a watch that does what it was meant for. Pace, distance, splits, a lap button you can hit with sweaty or frozen fingers, a battery that won’t quit at mile 20, and a screen you can read no matter how tired. That’s the job. These do the job.
They’re also—and this surprises people—what a lot of very fast runners wear. Stand near the front of a starting corral sometime and count the watches that cost less than the shoes. Elites don’t need a wrist device to tell them they’re tired. They need accurate splits.
If you’re new, that’s the biggest thing you need. Nothing kills a running habit faster than forty metrics you don’t understand that insist you’re doing it wrong. Same goes if you’re kitting out a kid for their first track or cross-country season: buy the simple device. It’ll survive the school bus, the mud, and the whole season. And they’ll learn to run by feel, which is the entire point. My first Garmin was essentially a pace-watching brick on my wrist and I still managed PRs. Here’s what I’d actually put on your wrist.

Wall Street’s initial optimism following Tuesday’s midterm elections quickly turned into a sharp selloff, driven largely by concerns about the future of AI and data-center investments. But beyond the market’s volatility, the election results sent a message that leaders in Washington and Jefferson City should take seriously: Americans want relief from rising costs and a more stable future.
Democrats made major gains in Congress as many people voiced frustration about the cost of living, economic uncertainty, and national and foreign policies. Missouri’s results also showed a changing political landscape. Democrats gained seats in the state legislature, while Republicans lost their supermajorities in Jefferson City.
These results should not be seen only as a win for one party or a sign of political gridlock. They offer a chance to rethink policies that affect Missouri’s workers, farmers, families, and businesses. And the economic concerns behind that opportunity are real, not speculative.
Months before the election, an August 2026 Saint Louis University/YouGov survey of 900 likely Missouri voters documented widespread financial anxiety. 69% worried about affording health care, 66% about groceries and gasoline, 62% about utility bills, and 59% about property taxes. Only 25% rated Missouri’s economy as good or excellent, while just 21% gave the national economy similarly positive marks. The same survey found that 68% opposed construction of a new data center in their community.
The war with Iran added to economic pressures. As I discussed in my March analysis and June follow-up, the conflict’s effects on energy markets, transportation costs, and economic uncertainty extend well beyond the Middle East, reaching Missouri families, farmers, and businesses. Those economic consequences have since become part of the broader political debate, with even administration officials acknowledging the war’s role in the midterm backlash.
These findings do not establish why every Missourian voted as they did. But they show that economic dissatisfaction and concerns about the costs of technological development were already widespread before Election Day. The challenge now is to translate the demand for change into policies that deliver meaningful economic improvements.

Tennessee regulators are warning about a growing “memo of sale” scam that can cost homeowners dearly and can complicate title and property insurance purchases.
The Tennessee Department of Commerce and Insurance, the state attorney general and others posted a bulletin this week that explained that, when sellers list their homes for sale, scammers may offer cash purchases. But instead of cash, the scammers will file a memorandum of sale with the clerk of court.
The memo notifies any other possible buyers about the pending sale and can prevent the homeowner from selling to another potential buyer, TDCI said in the bulletin. The scam company usually refuses to close on the sale, then demands a ransom of tens of thousands of dollars to clear the title.
“The homeowner is left with little recourse,” the department noted.
The scammers may claim to be real-estate wholesalers. But Tennessee regulations require that wholesalers must make “clear and conspicuous” disclosure of their intent to find third-party buyers, TDCI said.
The officials offered some words of advice for sellers:
- Pay attention to whether the sales contract contains language about recording a memorandum. Consider negotiating language that details when the memorandum will be removed.
- Ask clearly if the buyer intends to wholesale the property.
- Get everything in writing.
- Use TDCI’s Public Search to check the license status of the individual approaching the seller.
- If the buyer is demanding payment to release a memo, consult a licensed Tennessee attorney for guidance.
- File a complaint with the state Attorney General’s Office, Consumer Affairs Division
The department did not say how many sellers have been targeted by the scam.
